reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A slowly progressive distal myopathy typically presenting in early adulthood with foot drop and weakness of the tibialis anterior
Characteristically spares the quadriceps until late in the disease, a feature that helps distinguish it from many other myopathies
Inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and caused by mutations in GNE, the gene for the key enzyme of sialic acid biosynthesis
Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and cytoplasmic inclusions but characteristically lacks the inflammation of sporadic inclusion body myositis
Creatine kinase is usually normal or only modestly raised despite progressive weakness
Weakness advances proximally over years and can eventually affect the upper limbs and, later, the hip girdle, with relative sparing of facial and ocular muscles
Sialic acid replacement strategies have been investigated experimentally, so accurate genetic diagnosis is important for prognosis, counselling and trial eligibility
reference.pathophysiology: GNE myopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in GNE, which encodes the bifunctional enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase/N-acetylmannosamine kinase that catalyses the rate-limiting steps of sialic acid biosynthesis. Reduced enzyme activity leads to hyposialylation of muscle glycoproteins and glycolipids, which is thought to impair muscle-cell function and promote the accumulation of autophagic and protein aggregates seen histologically as rimmed vacuoles and inclusions. The resulting slow degeneration of muscle fibres produces the characteristic distal-onset, quadriceps-sparing pattern of weakness, although the precise link between hyposialylation and fibre loss is incompletely understood.
additionalDifferentials: Other distal myopathies such as Miyoshi myopathy
Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies with distal features
Chronic inflammatory or hereditary neuropathies causing foot drop
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase, typically normal or mildly elevated
Electromyography showing a myopathic pattern, sometimes with mixed features
Muscle magnetic resonance imaging to show the distal and quadriceps-sparing pattern of involvement
Muscle biopsy demonstrating rimmed vacuoles and inclusions without significant inflammation
Nerve conduction studies to exclude a neuropathic cause of foot drop
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an inflammatory rather than genetic myopathy
Prominent inflammation on biopsy that would favour sporadic inclusion body myositis
Respiratory muscle involvement in advanced disease
Loss of ambulation requiring mobility and falls assessment
reference.prognosis: GNE myopathy is slowly progressive, with many patients losing independent ambulation roughly one to two decades after onset, but life expectancy is usually preserved as respiratory and cardiac involvement are uncommon and generally late.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as sporadic inclusion body myositis and treating with immunotherapy, which is ineffective
Being reassured by a normal creatine kinase and dismissing a genetic myopathy
Attributing the foot drop to a peripheral neuropathy without recognising the myopathic pattern
Overlooking the characteristic quadriceps sparing that points to the diagnosis
